selected.name: Global closure of local alternatives
selected.instruction: Score 10 when pointwise possibilities are shown to combine into one globally consistent form, with mixed assignments explicitly ruled out; score 0 when the post stops after listing possibilities for each individual input.
selected.rationale: Rows R16 and R25 first obtain the pointwise alternatives 0, x^2, and -x^2, then address the essential mixed-pattern obstruction. This is evidence of solving the global problem rather than only deriving local constraints.

selected.name: Global coverage of cases
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the argument explicitly covers every permitted parameter range, branch, parity, or exceptional case; score 0 when it handles only a convenient subcase or a single example.
selected.rationale: R34 and R60 cover all n through intervals and parity cases, while R15 and R37 rely on one narrowly chosen situation.
member_names: Overlapping interval coverage for universal quantification

selected.name: Self-labels own method as hacky or non-rigorous
selected.instruction: Score whether the poster explicitly characterizes their own method, in their own words, as a shortcut, hack, guess, or non-genuine solve (e.g., 'troll solution', 'fakesolve', 'cheap but fast', 'ridiculous... overkill', 'scuffed'). A 10: the post never characterizes its own technique this way; it is presented (rightly or wrongly) as a genuine solution. A 0: the poster explicitly flags their own approach with this kind of self-deprecating or hedging label.
selected.rationale: R12 opens with 'Scuffed troll solution', R53 is tagged '[hide=fakesolve]', R39 calls its own method 'ridiculous and yet ultimately equivalent... overkill', and R7 is labeled a 'cheap but fast solution' — all four carry unusually low dense_pct (0.274, 0.056, 0.140, 0.324, respectively) despite mostly high card_pct, a consistent pattern across four separate rows.
member_names: Disclaims the legitimacy of its own method
Post self-brands its route as a deviation or a stunt
Self-labels own method as hacky or non-rigorous

selected.name: Completeness of candidate classification
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the post both derives all possible candidates and directly verifies that each candidate satisfies the original conditions; score 0 when it guesses candidates, verifies only some, or never excludes alternatives.
selected.rationale: R02 and R42 classify and check all functional-equation solutions, whereas R28 and R25 give conclusions with little candidate analysis.

selected.name: Generalizes beyond the minimum needed
selected.instruction: Score whether the post goes beyond exactly what is needed to answer the stated problem, e.g. by extending the argument to a broader family (different n, different configuration), stating additional properties of the configuration, or adding a labeled 'further observations' section. A 10: the post clearly extends its reasoning or findings beyond the minimal answer, with the extension clearly marked as bonus/general material. A 0: the post stops the instant the requested quantity is obtained, with no exploration of the broader structure.
selected.rationale: R20 solves the specific 10-move triangle question quickly, then extends its method to general n-gon random walks and takes a limit as k→∞; R48 answers the requested AB^2 and then adds an 'Other Observations' section on the K-symmedian and the P-Dumpty point. Both carry high dense_pct (0.865, 0.762) despite low card_pct.
member_names: Engages structure beyond the question asked
Explores the configuration beyond the minimum needed

selected.name: Explicit claim-proof structuring
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the solution contains multiple explicitly labeled claims or lemmas (using 'Claim:', 'Lemma:', or equivalent markers), each with its own proof block. Score 0 if the solution is unstructured flowing prose or raw calculations with no organizational markers.
selected.rationale: R07, R45, R49, R57, R60 (dense_high) use labeled claim-proof structure. R03, R18, R29 (dense_low) lack such structure. The scorecard may not weight this organizational hallmark heavily enough.

selected.name: Exact modular periodicity
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the post proves a valid period or residue restriction and then uses it exhaustively to constrain the target; score 0 when it merely reports a pattern or invokes a modulus without justifying all relevant cases.
selected.rationale: R10 uses parity and modulo 3 cycles, R17 uses root-of-unity periodicity, and R40 combines congruences to exclude all larger cases.
member_names: Recurrence identification with modular parity analysis

selected.name: Named inequality equality case exploitation
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the solution explicitly identifies the equality case of a named inequality (Cauchy-Schwarz, AM-GM, Jensen, Minkowski, etc.) and uses this equality condition to determine the answer. Score 0 if no named inequality equality case is identified or used.
selected.rationale: R05 (dense_high) identifies the Cauchy-Schwarz equality case to determine side-length ratios. R34 (dense_low) mentions convexity but never completes the argument or identifies the extremal case.

selected.name: Names and separately addresses a trap or edge case
selected.instruction: Score whether the post explicitly names a specific trap, degenerate configuration, or edge case (rather than only implicitly handling it inside general casework) and pauses to address it as its own labeled step. A 10: a specific trap/edge case is explicitly named (e.g., 'the pointwise trap', 'if a=b this fails', 'the degenerate case where...') and separately resolved. A 0: no edge case or trap is ever explicitly named as such, even if some casework is present.
selected.rationale: R24 has a section explicitly headed 'We now deal with the pointwise trap' with three enumerated subcases; R31 structures its final claims (Claims 2-4) explicitly around ruling out specific degenerate value-pairings the pointwise ambiguity could produce. Both carry high dense_pct (0.921 and 0.817) with low card_pct.
member_names: Degenerate or pitfall branch identified and killed
Names and closes the known failure mode of its own route
Names and separately addresses a trap or edge case

selected.name: Exploits the multiple-choice option list
selected.instruction: For posts on problems that display answer choices (A)-(E). 10 = the post determines the answer as a value, never using the option list except to report the letter at the end. 0 = the option list is load-bearing: the post computes a residue or parity and picks the unique surviving choice, or argues that the choices are far enough apart that a coarse computation distinguishes them, or works in a substitute setting on the grounds that the listed answers are distinguishable there. Score 5 if the option list is used only as a final sanity check on an independently obtained value. Score 5 for problems with no answer choices.
selected.rationale: R52 (dense 0.324, card 0.886) admits it is 'very cheap' and selects the only choice that is odd and 1 mod 3; R44 (dense 0.140, card 0.848) argues explicitly that 'the answer choices are all clearly distinct and extant over F_25' and then works there; R23 (dense 0.274, card 0.923) approximates its way to a neighbourhood of 72 and reads off a choice. All three are card-top and dense-low, so the scorecard is crediting a shortcut that does not answer the underlying question.
member_names: Computes the asked quantity rather than eliminating options

selected.name: Notation and equation consistency
selected.instruction: Score 10 when symbols, indices, signs, substitutions, and displayed equations remain consistent throughout; score 0 when notation changes, equations contain unexplained typos, or later steps do not follow from earlier ones.
selected.rationale: R06 and R18 maintain a coherent sequence of functional identities, while R10 and R22 contain visible notation or formula inconsistencies.

selected.name: Independent-choice encoding
selected.instruction: Score 10 when each object is assigned to an independent slot or state and the correspondence is shown to be bijective, yielding the count; score 0 when a product or sum is asserted without explaining what its terms represent.
selected.rationale: Rows R06 and R52 encode subset growth and binary expansions through independent placement choices and products. The criterion detects whether a compact count faithfully represents the original objects.

selected.name: Names the pivotal idea in plain words
selected.instruction: Score whether the post explicitly identifies the one hinge on which the problem turns, in words a reader could repeat, independent of whether the post executes anything. 10 = the hinge is stated outright as a sentence or a displayed identity: 'F_{2n}/F_n = F_{n+1}+F_{n-1}', 'the problem is equivalent to minimizing AI_1 * AI_2, and AI_1*AI_2 = AX*AI so minimize AX', 'the monovariant is the difference between the largest and smallest a_i'. 0 = the post performs computation or case analysis from which a reader could not extract any statement of what the key idea was. Terseness must not be penalized and length must not be rewarded: a one-line post that states the hinge scores 10.
selected.rationale: R03 (dense 0.817, card 0.121) is one identity plus self-deprecation; R13 (dense 0.778, card 0.108) is a three-line sketch that names the reduction; R43 (dense 0.684, card 0.053) and R22 (dense 0.638, card 0.045) contain no executed mathematics at all yet name the monovariant / the induction quantity in prose. All four are dense-high and card-bottom, so the scorecard appears to be measuring executed work and missing idea-naming.
member_names: Names the pivotal idea in plain words
Pivotal idea named in standard terms, execution aside

selected.name: Construction admissibility
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a constructed object is checked to be integral, distinct, ordered, and within every stated domain restriction, as well as satisfying the defining relations; score 0 when formulas are presented without these checks.
selected.rationale: R03 checks prime-factor and size restrictions, while R56 and R57 verify that constructed triples lie in the card interval and have the required pairwise sums.

selected.name: Single external theorem does all the work
selected.instruction: Score how much of the argument is discharged by invoking one heavy named or external result whose statement is not proved or unpacked in the post. 10 = no such invocation; every step is carried out on the objects of the problem. 0 = essentially the whole problem is dispatched by one citation - the hook-length formula for Young tableaux (with a link), Minkowski's inequality applied once to get the answer, a scaling trick that manufactures the answer in two lines - so that the post contains almost no reasoning specific to this problem. Mid scores when a named result is invoked but substantial problem-specific work surrounds it.
selected.rationale: R29 (dense 0.254, card 0.953) is a single hook-length citation with an external URL; R32 (dense 0.268, card 0.901) is one application of Minkowski; R33 (dense 0.108, card 0.729) is a one-shot scaling construction. All three are near the top of the scorecard and near the bottom of the dense ranking, so a rubric that credits correctness and concision will over-reward exactly this shape.
member_names: One cited heavyweight theorem does all the work
Single external theorem does all the work

selected.name: Colloquial and emotional register
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text uses informal colloquial language, slang, self-deprecation, emoticons, or emotional interjections (e.g., 'rip', 'cuz', ':(', 'nooooo', 'Bro'), as opposed to standard mathematical prose. 0 = entirely formal; 10 = heavily colloquial/emotional. Do not judge whether informality is good or bad.
selected.rationale: R01 ('I assumed... didn't really know why... :(') and R22 ('Bro... cuz im dumb... RIP') are dense_high_card_low: the dense model may key on approach content while the scorecard is put off by register. R09 ('Dangit') and R25 ('Holy cow') show the same split.
member_names: Casual affect, interjections and self-deprecating chatter

selected.name: Legacy autocorrupted LaTeX and era-marked forum markup
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post carries typographic markers of an older era of this forum's software, judged purely by their presence. Count: math macros of the form backslash-equal-brace-brace and backslash-minus-brace-brace appearing where a plain equals sign or minus sign belongs; a stray space immediately after an opening dollar sign (for example a dollar sign followed by space then a numeral); bracketed url tags with a full http address inside the prose; double-square-bracket wiki-style links or File inclusions; hide tags whose argument is wrapped in double quotes rather than bare; and other markup that is not the modern plain form. 0 = none of these appear; 10 = they appear throughout. Do NOT judge whether old or new markup is better, cleaner or more readable, and do NOT judge the mathematics. Score only how much era-marked markup is visibly present.
selected.rationale: Pure dating artifact with zero bearing on which solution route is taken. R01 contains both the corrupted equals macro and a bracketed http url tag; R14 contains the corrupted minus and equals macros; R12 and R35 show the spaced-dollar-sign habit of the same period. A text-only model can read the decade off these tokens, so they are a live nuisance channel; nothing about them says anything about approach.
member_names: Era-marked markup, notation and link style
Legacy autocorrupted LaTeX and era-marked forum markup

selected.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of explicit references to collaborators, helpers, prior assistance, or thanking another participant; do not judge the value of that assistance.
selected.rationale: Collaboration leaves visible attribution traces and may also influence which route the author adopts, making this mixed. Examples include R16, R34, and R53.

selected.name: Structured claim-proof formatting
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text uses structured formatting elements typical of olympiad-style write-ups: labeled Claims, color-coded or bold headers, italicized 'Proof.' markers, or section dividers (e.g., horizontal rules). 0 = plain prose with no structural markers; 10 = extensive use of such elements throughout. Do not judge whether such formatting improves the solution.
selected.rationale: R13, R32, R35, R36, and R51 all deploy colored bold claim headers and are dense_high_card_low, suggesting the dense model responds to content while the scorecard may discount or the reverse. R19 and R24 (dense_low_card_high) also use heavy formatting, showing the feature cuts both ways and is predictive of disagreement.
member_names: Forum markup furniture: hide blocks, colour-tagged claims, boxed answers

selected.name: Validation-seeking and uncertain posture
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post is framed as a question, request for checking, or expression of doubt rather than a confident solution. Look for phrases like 'Does this work?', 'Can someone please explain why', 'Wouldn't that be overcounting?', or 'I'm getting X, is this right?'. Do not judge whether the uncertainty is warranted; score only how much the text seeks validation.
selected.rationale: A post can contain substantial mathematics yet be framed as an inquiry, which may inflate a checklist score without matching the canonical approach. R18 asks 'Does this work?'; R37 asks 'Can someone please explain why 391 is incorrect?'; R38 asks 'Wouldn't that be overcounting?'
member_names: Help-seeking and uncertainty posture toward one's own post

selected.name: Explicit self-assessment labels
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post labels its own solution with qualitative descriptors such as 'cheap', 'fast', 'overkill', 'scuffed', 'troll', 'cursed', 'different', 'alternative', or 'simple'. Do not judge whether the label is accurate; score only how many such self-assessment phrases appear.
selected.rationale: Self-labeling can bias a scorer independently of the actual mathematical approach. R09 calls itself 'very cheap but fast'; R40 says 'Scuffed troll solution'; R54 says 'cursed solution which somehow got a 7/7'; R04 calls itself 'a different solution'.

selected.name: Explicit citation of or engagement with an external/wiki reference
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post text itself names or links to an outside reference -- e.g. an embedded [url=...] link, the phrase 'wiki solution', 'the wiki', or otherwise explicitly naming an external write-up it is drawing on or questioning. 0 = no such citation anywhere in the text; 10 = the post is centrally built around naming or quoting an external reference. Do not judge whether the citation is accurate or the linked material authoritative -- score only whether this citing language appears in the text.
selected.rationale: R21 embeds a '[url=...Young_tableau...]hook-length formula[/url]' link and R24 opens with 'I am confused on the wiki solution #2 for this' -- both are textual, in-post citations (not judge-side comparisons); it is mixed because a post that explicitly engages the wiki write-up may also be more likely to actually track its approach.
member_names: Explicit citation of or engagement with an external/wiki reference

selected.name: Back-reference language presupposing earlier posts in the thread
selected.instruction: Read only the problem and this one post. Score 0-10 how much of the post's language presupposes that other posts already exist in this thread and positions this post relative to them. Count: direct address to another poster ('@above', 'thanks!', 'his monovariant'); phrases such as 'similar to above', 'different from the others', 'I already addressed this in my previous post', 'as I said', 'the wiki solution #2', 'Solution 2', 'another way'; a reply that continues an argument the reader cannot see; and any sentence that would be incoherent if this were the first post. 0 = the post engages the bare problem as though nothing had been said yet; 10 = nearly every sentence leans on unseen prior posts. You must NOT judge whether back-reference is good, polite, helpful or lazy, must NOT judge the mathematics, and must NOT try to guess what the earlier posts said. Score only the visible extent of back-reference language.
selected.rationale: Arrival position is not approach-match, but it leaves a loud lexical trace and plausibly co-varies with how a post is scored by a text-only model. R41 opens '@above that is listing everything out', R46 opens '@above thanks!', R14 is entirely a reply ('Um no, I already addressed this in my previous post'), R43 says 'here's my solution similar to above', R36 says 'I am confused on the wiki solution #2', and R03 self-describes as 'different from the others'. None of these markers is evidence about which route the write-up takes; they are timestamps in disguise. Tagged mixed because a poster arriving late may also genuinely be pushed toward an off-canonical route.
member_names: Back-reference language presupposing earlier posts in the thread
Backward reference to earlier thread activity

selected.name: Answer-extraction framing versus proof framing in the item
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which this item is framed as short answer-extraction rather than as sustained proof. Consider both halves of what you are shown: whether the problem block displays a lettered option bank (A) through (E) or asks for a single numeric quantity such as m+n, and whether the post terminates in a boxed or lettered final answer, uses phrasing like 'the answer is' or 'our answer is', reasons by elimination among the given options, or resolves in a handful of lines. 0 = an open-ended prove-or-show item answered by extended argument; 10 = an option-bank or numeric-answer item resolved to a boxed answer. Do NOT judge whether short answers or long proofs are better, harder or more valuable, and do NOT judge correctness. Score only the extent of answer-extraction framing.
selected.rationale: Problem kind is a property of the container the post landed in, not of the post's own approach, yet it is fully visible in the text and so is a strong text-only confound. R01, R23, R24, R28, R41, R48, R53 and R60 all sit under lettered option banks and end in a lettered or boxed answer, and R50 and R58 resolve numeric-answer items in a few lines; R02, R30, R32, R39 and R42 sit under 'Prove that' or 'Show that' statements with no answer to extract. Tagged mixed because the number of genuinely distinct viable routes really does depend on problem kind.
member_names: Answer-extraction framing versus proof framing in the item
Multiple-choice answer-extraction framing in the post

selected.rationale: R12 explicitly corrects an answer choice, R33 identifies choice C, and R46 dismisses choice E. These visible test-taking conventions can affect reception without indicating the substantive solution approach.
